title: Task Initiation: The 2-Minute Rule
text: When you feel paralyzed to start a task, commit to doing it for just 2 minutes. The hardest part of an ADHD task is the initiation phase (executive dysfunction). Tell yourself, 'I will only work on this for 120 seconds.' Once you start, the brain's dopamine kicks in and you often find it easy to keep going past the 2-minute mark.
source_citation: Task decomposition as a module of Safren's CBT for adult ADHD: Safren, S. A., Perlman, C. A., Sprich, S., & Otto, M. W. (2017). Mastering Your Adult ADHD: A Cognitive-Behavioral Treatment Program (2nd ed.). Oxford University Press.

title: Working Memory: The Launchpad Strategy
text: Working memory deficits cause us to forget where we put things. Create a 'launchpad' by the door: a single physical spot where keys, wallet, and phone must live every day. Do not put them in your pocket or on the kitchen counter. The ritual of placing them on the launchpad prevents morning ADHD panic.
source_citation: Externalized memory / 'home for every object' — widely recommended in adult ADHD coaching (CHADD; Understood.org). No single named RCT; standard consequence of working-memory deficits in Barkley's model.

title: Time Blindness: Visual Timers
text: ADHD involves 'time blindness' — the inability to sense how much time has passed, a term and concept described by ADHD researcher Dr. Russell Barkley. Use analog wall clocks or visual timers (like a Time Timer) where the red wedge physically disappears. Do not rely on your internal clock or your phone screen (which is full of distractions). Make time visible.
source_citation: Barkley, R. A. (2022). Taking Charge of Adult ADHD: Proven Strategies to Succeed at Work, at Home, and in Relationships (2nd ed.). Guilford Press. 'Time blindness' is Barkley's own term.

title: Rejection Sensitive Dysphoria: Pausing Before Reacting
text: Rejection Sensitive Dysphoria (RSD) — a term coined by Dr. William Dodson, though it is not an official clinical diagnosis — describes intense emotional pain from perceived criticism. When you feel a sudden wave of shame or anger, it can help not to act on it immediately. Step away, breathe, and write down the facts versus the feelings before responding to anything upsetting (an email, a text, a comment). Often the perceived rejection is a misinterpretation of a neutral or ambiguous cue.
source_citation: Dodson, W. (coined 'RSD'). Note: RSD is not an official DSM-5 diagnosis. 'Pause before responding' is a generic emotion-regulation coping step; no source names a specific 'rule' attached to it.

title: Body Doubling
text: Body doubling is the practice of working alongside another person (physically or virtually) to stay focused. Many people with ADHD report the presence of a low-stakes witness helps them start and stay on task, though it is worth noting that body doubling is widely reported anecdotally rather than something with controlled research behind exactly how or why it works. If you can't find someone to sit with you, a 'Study with Me' video on YouTube can simulate the effect for some people.
source_citation: Understood.org / CHADD / ADDA all describe body doubling but explicitly characterise the evidence as anecdotal ('almost no research'). Treat as widely-reported strategy, not validated treatment.

title: Reducing Distractions: Out of Sight, Out of Mind
text: Removing the sources of distraction from your environment — and adding friction to the ones you cannot remove — is a well-established behavioural technique often called stimulus control. In ADHD-adapted CBT it is usually framed as 'out of sight, out of mind': keep your phone in another room while working, log out of social apps, put snacks on a high shelf, and keep the TV remote in a drawer. The point is not to 'be disciplined' — it is to reduce the number of moments where you have to spend willpower choosing not to get distracted. Willpower is finite; environment design is not.
source_citation: Stimulus control as a foundational behavioural principle (Skinner, B. F., 1953, Science and Human Behavior), applied in ADHD-adapted CBT (Safren et al., 2010, JAMA 304(8):875-880) and recommended in Barkley, R. A. (2022), Taking Charge of Adult ADHD (2nd ed.).

title: Cognitive Restructuring for ADHD-Specific Thoughts
text: Cognitive restructuring, a core technique in Dr. Steven Safren's CBT protocol for adult ADHD ('Mastering Your Adult ADHD'), focuses on changing negative self-talk. When you think 'I am lazy,' reframe it to 'I have executive dysfunction, and my brain struggles to initiate.' This is not an excuse; it reflects how ADHD affects the brain. Changing the narrative from moral failure to neurological difference can reduce shame and improve task engagement. A 2010 randomised controlled trial (Safren et al., JAMA) found CBT combined with medication more effective than medication alone for adult ADHD symptoms.
source_citation: Safren, S. A., Sprich, S., Mimiaga, M. J., et al. (2010). Cognitive behavioral therapy vs relaxation with educational support for medication-treated adults with ADHD and persistent symptoms: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA, 304(8), 875-880. doi:10.1001/jama.2010.1272

title: Behavioral Activation
text: ADHD brains often struggle with the 'motivation follows action' rule — we wait to 'feel like' doing something before we do it. Behavioral Activation, a component of ADHD-adapted CBT protocols, teaches the opposite: do the action first, and motivation will often follow. Start with the smallest possible physical movement (e.g., just opening the laptop), and let momentum build from there.
source_citation: Behavioral Activation is a component of ADHD-adapted CBT protocols (e.g., the CADDI protocol built on Safren et al., 2010, JAMA).

title: Habit Stacking
text: To build a new habit, anchor it to an existing automatic routine. This technique, popularised as 'Habit Stacking' by James Clear in Atomic Habits (building on B. J. Fogg's 'Tiny Habits' concept), is commonly recommended as ADHD-friendly because it does not rely on remembering a new habit on its own. The formula is: 'After [CURRENT HABIT], I will [NEW HABIT].' For example: 'After I brush my teeth, I will take my medication.' Because the existing habit is already automatic, the new habit piggybacks on that routine instead of needing its own trigger.
source_citation: Clear, J. (2018). Atomic Habits. Avery. Building on Fogg, B. J. (2019). Tiny Habits. Popular self-help strategy — not from CHADD / Safren / Barkley clinical literature.
